h1: Turning Loose Thoughts into Shareable Writing
p: A Writing Tool for Thinkers, Not Writers
We’re a team of four designers trying to ship a writing tool for thinkers whose thoughts are rich but struggle to shape them into cohesive and logical writing.
Right now, we’re living with our coded prototypes and iterating quickly as we learn.
It’s still a work in progress, but we’re excited to share the final build soon.
Meanwhile, here are some snippets of things we’ve been concepting, prototyping, and vibe-coding.

/2025/icebreaker.title: Bruce Cao | Design Portfolio
p: One Week to Melt the Ice

I was challenged to design a Google Meet feature that makes icebreakers smoother and less awkward for groups who don’t know each other well. In one week, I created a feature called Floating Notes, a lightweight, playful mode built directly into the Meet grid.
The concept earned strong, direct praise from an ex-Google UX designer.
Icebreakers often end up feeling like the coldest part of the meeting.

Most icebreakers become a quiet stare at a single question slide. People are so busy crafting their answer and bracing for the spotlight that they barely look at each other. This turns what should be a human moment into something cold and forgettable.
How do we make faces & presence—not slides—the center of attention?

Online interactions feel colder, making it easy to hide behind slides, sidebars, and the tiny group tile. The challenge was to design something that naturally pulls attention back to faces, reactions, and presence.
How do we make the space feel low-stress and expressive?
Icebreakers shouldn’t feel like pop quizzes or punchline contests. We needed a playful, low-pressure environment where personality can come through in more than just spoken words.
How do we solve the “memory loss” problem?
People immediately forget what the first person said. We needed lightweight interactions that help participants actually remember each other.
How do we give facilitators smoother control?

Timing and transitions are messy, and facilitators often feel impolite in interrupting someone. The system needed a clearer structure, smoother handoffs, and settings that could be configured upfront but still adapt as the session evolved.
Turning the Grid Into a Sharing Circle

Instead of adding new panels or side tools, I connected the center of the Meet grid into a “question island.”This transforms the screen into a circle where everyone can actually see each other’s reactions while sharing, making the moment warmer, more human, and less awkward.
Floating Notes for Playful, Interactive Expression

Participants answer with customizable cards that support text, emojis, photos, and simple doodles. No screen-sharing needed.Hovering over someone brings their card forward, allowing quick glances and helping people actually remember each other.
No one wants to be the awkward first speaker. Let Gemini kick things off with a light, humorous, or silly answer that sets the tone and lowers the collective pressure.
A Pre-Set Flow With Easy On-the-Spot Adjustments
Facilitators configure timing and order in advance, and can manually adjust anything during the session as needed.
The concept received strong, direct validation from an ex-Google UX designer, who emphasized how surprisingly effective the simplicity of the idea was.
My biggest takeaway: solutions don’t always need to be complex. When we focus on one real pain point and shape our solution around it, the result can feel fresh, intuitive, and genuinely human.

/2025/adit.title: Bruce Cao | Design Portfolio
h1: Enabling Snackable Moments of Visual Creativity
p: Turn Idle Moments into Creative Expression

Adit was created during a five-day designathon with the theme of transforming idle moments into creativity. We presented to a panel of 15 industry designers in New York from places like Apple, Notion, Meta, Google Creative Lab, New.Computer, Avara, and more.
We got laughs, nods, and were urged to ship it as an actual app.
Remix The Subway Ads Around You

Adit turns every subway ad into a hijackable canvas for those boring minutes waiting for the train. Whether the users are seriously redesigning or casually memeing, it gives them a natural outlet for humor, irony, and creativity.
Design a Lightweight Editor on a Tiny Screen

Graphic editing on mobile is notoriously clunky—precision actions, multi-finger inputs, and complex settings don’t apply. We needed a tool that frictionlessly transforms spontaneous thoughts into polished visuals.
Design for the Underground Void, with Low or Zero Signal
NYC subways are where internet dreams get buried. We had to imagine how a visual editor could still function when the rest of the internet stalls.
Make Adit More Than a One-Ride Joke

We didn’t want people to edit one ad, giggle, and delete the app. Our challenge was to give Adit a social loop and community value so riders would return, share, and participate during their daily commute.
A Minimal Toolkit Demands Nothing More Than Your Thumbs

We built a lightweight editor powered by doodle-based AI prompts—circle something, write a phrase, and the system handles complex edits.Adit also preloads existing brand palettes, fonts, and brand materials for each ad, making execution fast with nearly no manual precision.
An AI Prompting System Syncs to the Subway’s Stop-and-Go Rhythm

Because the signal is strongest at stations, Adit uses an asynchronous distribution queue: it reminds users to send prompts at one stop, and results arrive at the next. The server will handle the requests on its side in between.
We tied the loading bar to real train-running data, so you know when your AI edits will be sent back.
Local Station Feeds and Community Creativity
Adit features a station-based feed highlighting top remixes, voting, and playful interactions. Users can save their ads, build a personal “artist profile,” and tap into a hyperlocal creative culture.

We pitched Adit as a punk, NYC-born creative tool—and it landed.The panel responded with laughter, enthusiasm, and a lively debate on its future direction. We were urged to actually build and ship it for its cultural potential.
“I love that you respect the time underground... It’s awesome that you have that interaction while you’re between each stops thought out. Those little things make the experience so much better.”

/2025/lore.title: Bruce Cao | Design Portfolio
p: A 0-1 Product, 6 Weeks, 3 Designers, $10M Fund Raise

Lore was a pre-seed startup that grew out of the founders’ love for rabbit-holing—getting lost in a topic or fandom for hours. Their goal was to build an infrastructure-level platform for fan rabbit-holing.We acted as Lore’s founding design team, transforming a vague vision for “magical rabbit-holing” into a clear product direction and high-fidelity prototypes.
These prototypes helped Lore successfully raise $10M during their seed round.

The founders came to us convinced that the fan experience is fractured. Rabbit-holing may start with a spark on social media, but digging deeper sends users bouncing between wikis, Reddit threads, videos, and scattered articles.
Users are constantly switching context, questioning authenticity, getting distracted, and losing momentum.
People currently jump between fragmented searches, wiki tabs, and Reddit threads, making it hard to retrace steps.

User preferences for the length and format of information vary over the course of a rabbit-holing experience. Some sub-topics call for a 2-hour YouTube documentary, some sub-topics just require a simple summary to move forward.
Balance Facts, Theories, and Community Insight
Fans shift between wanting factual clarity, fan theories, and community sentiment at different moments. We needed a structure that supported diverse content types.
A Seamless Entry Point From Social Media
The Lore Companion brings your initial context directly into Lore, reducing fragmentation and allowing you to stay within one continuous rabbit hole.
Building in Passive Ways to Follow Up
Users can actively ask follow-up questions or passively extend content through simple interactions like dragging for more detail.
Tuning The Rhythm of Your Rabbit-holing
A built-in media converter lets users toggle between formats, such as turning a long text result into a precisely timestamped video explanation.
Battle Bars visualize reactions pulled from social and fan platforms, turning community debates into interactive prompts for deeper exploration.
We delivered both low-fidelity mechanics and a high-fidelity, whimsical investor vision. Lore raised $10M in their seed round.
“This is the first time the Lore team has worked with folks who took our notes and delivered instantaneously—truly above and beyond.”
